en: An IOC ecosystem can be described as a technical-organizational arrangement that sustains and conditions enjoyment over time, integrating continued operation, private governance and update cycles that define, in practical terms, what counts as admissible use, recognized performance, displayable collection and position preserved or degraded in the system.<1>p. 485</1>

Inside the game, six categories serve to identify which dimension a modulation has affected. They are cosmetic-ornamental objects, progression objects, access and permanence objects, functionality objects, time objects and reputation objects. The typology is internal to that laboratory and is not a general classification of platforms, and a concrete object may combine more than one category. Outside it, the move to general parameters is not made by extrapolation but by the functional equivalence of governance mechanisms, with explicit conceptual lenses and reconstruction through elements attributable to the supplier and publicly retrievable, such as update logs, stated reasons for change, access policies and sanction criteria. It does not follow that every continuous digital service falls within this framework. Software, accounts, libraries and tools under continuous provision tend to be the most evident cases.

Generalization, here, does not occur through impressionistic extrapolation, but through controlled transit between levels of abstraction, guided by the functional equivalence of mechanisms of governance by architecture.<1>p. 497</1>

The legally relevant point does not lie in asserting that every continuous digital service is subject to the same framework, nor in expanding the concept on the mere argument of the digitalization of economic life.<1>p. 713</1>

Thus, the removal or relevant degradation of essential functionality in editing software, the unjustified restriction of access to an account that concentrates files and libraries, or the substantial alteration of the conditions of use of contracted tools may affect the very object enjoyed, and not merely an accessory convenience of the service.<1>p. 713</1>
The typology mobilized here is neither sectoral nor merely technological.<1>p. 713</1>

The constitutional order and the sectoral framework
What power does the legal order need to see when the platform governs enjoyment?

In ecosystems of continued enjoyment, the conflict no longer fits the image of a contractual disagreement or of shifting preferences, because the value of the object depends on an administered environment in which visibility, reputation, access, permanence and sanction are distributed by internal criteria, mainly through architectural and informational means. This ordering has a name. The law of the platform articulates terms of use, community standards, interfaces, visibility hierarchies, enforcement systems, which is the application of the rules by the platform itself, update routines, evidence regimes and customer service practices into a unitary practical normativity. It is not a metaphor to ornament the digital but an analytical category, whose core lies in the coordination of these mechanisms and in the effects they produce on who gains access, how they remain, what can be lost and on what terms the loss can be contested.

The reorganization of immaterial consumption around governed ecosystems makes it insufficient to treat the conflict as a simple contractual disagreement or as a fluctuation of individual preferences. The enjoyment that sustains the value of the IOC depends on an administered environment in which visibility, reputation, access, permanence and sanction are distributed according to internal criteria, by predominantly architectural and informational means.<1>p. 347</1>

It is on this plane that it becomes necessary to name the Lex Plataformae. The expression designates the private ordering through which the platform structures and governs the enjoyment of the Immaterial Object of Consumption, articulating terms of use, community standards, interfaces, visibility hierarchies, enforcement systems, update routines, evidence regimes and customer service practices into a unitary practical normativity.<1>p. 503</1>

It is not a metaphor to ornament the digital, but an analytical category aimed at making legally visible what would otherwise appear fragmented among contract, technique and everyday operation. Its core lies not in an isolated instrument nor in a specific algorithm, but in the institutional coordination of heterogeneous mechanisms that produce consistent normative effects on who gains access, how they remain, what can be perceived, what can be lost and on what terms the loss may be understood or contested.<1>p. 503</1>

When the platform concentrates the modulation of access, the reorganization of visibility, the alteration of the conditions of use, the filtering of evidence and the definition of the channels of contestation, the problem becomes one of the institutionalized exercise of private economic power over positions of continued enjoyment, and the asymmetry is not only informational or economic but also semiotic, the subject of the chapter on semiotic vulnerability. The response does not call for a rupture with the existing order but for a more demanding reading of its premises, because private power no longer operates only through price or clause but through the coordination of architecture, curation, sanction and ordinary management of the environment. Consumer protection as a fundamental right and a principle of the economic order is enough to frame these private forms of government, and the Constitution, the CDC and intellectual property come in as sources summoned by the same problem. The aim is not to moralize business choices but to produce decidable categories.

When the platform concentrates faculties of modulating access, reorganizing visibility, altering the conditions of use, filtering evidence and defining in practice the channels of contestation, the problem ceases to be merely that of supplying a good or service in a static sense and becomes that of the institutionalized exercise of private economic power over positions of continued enjoyment. The constitutional reading of the market, therefore, does not serve here as a decorative frame, but as a criterion of intelligibility and limitation.<1>p. 502</1>

In ecosystems of continued enjoyment, value is not exhausted in the initial delivery, because it depends on the persistence of technical, symbolic and organizational conditions that remain under the supplier's control. The utility consumed is realized over time, under permanent updating and curation, so that the consumer's vulnerability does not arise only from a lack of information about the object's characteristics, but also from structural dependence on the signs, metrics, interfaces and framings through which that object becomes intelligible, comparable and verifiable. It is precisely this administered dependence that makes it possible to understand why, on platforms, the asymmetry is not merely informational or economic in the classical sense, but also semiotic.<1>p. 503</1>

Private power, in this context, no longer operates only through the setting of prices or the drafting of clauses, but through the coordination of architecture, curation, sanction and ordinary management of the consumption environment. This mutation does not require a rupture with the existing legal order, but a more demanding reading of its own premises. Consumer protection as a fundamental right and a principle of the economic order already offers sufficient basis to frame, without artificiality, private forms of government that produce broad and repeated effects on the experience of enjoyment, even though they are not to be confused with state power.<1>p. 502</1>

The Constitution, the Consumer Protection Code and the intellectual property regimes do not apply here as watertight blocks, competing for abstract primacy, but as sources simultaneously summoned by one and the same legal problem.<1>p. 503</1>

The aim is not to moralize business choices nor to dissolve the technical specificity of these ecosystems into generic formulas of abuse. What is sought, rather, is to produce decidable categories, capable of bringing back into controllable legal language what, in the ordinary functioning of platforms, usually appears as mere technical necessity, a rule of the system or an inevitable consequence of the infrastructure.<1>p. 504</1>
Why does limiting this power not depend on treating it as public power?

The first support comes from The Right to Privacy, an article by Samuel D. Warren and Louis D. Brandeis published in 1890 in the Harvard Law Review. Faced with recent inventions and business practices that intensified intrusion, the authors defended a right to be let alone, distinct from defamation and literary property, and described the invasion of private life as an industry in which supply itself manufactures demand. The article is used methodologically, because technical change alters the conditions of exposure, harm and vulnerability and requires adjusting the categories, and the argument does not depend on an institutional transplant of the common law, the Anglo-American legal tradition, because the point is to readjust categories when the available frame becomes anachronistic. Transposed to the platform, the core of the problem lies not in isolated breaches but in a private governance infrastructure capable of organizing at scale the conditions of participation and enjoyment.
The recourse to Warren and Brandeis does not operate by thematic identity, but by homology of situation.<1>p. 348</1>

Entitled The Right to Privacy, the seminal article by Samuel D. Warren and Louis D. Brandeis <1>([201-?])</1>, originally published by the Harvard Law Review in 1890, formulates a matrix of legal reconstruction in the face of technical and social mutations that alter conditions of exposure, vulnerability and harm.<2>p. 347</2>

In their article, Warren and Brandeis <1>([201-?])</1> argue that recent inventions and expanding business practices intensified forms of intrusion that the legal order, if it remains tied to earlier schemes, cannot adequately capture. From there, the authors defend the recognition of a right to privacy as a legitimate right to be let alone, distinguishing it from adjacent institutions that protect different goods, such as defamation, aimed at reputation before third parties, and literary/authorial property, aimed at the economic exploitation of publication.<2>p. 347-348</2>

Warren and Brandeis describe the invasion of private life as an industry, pursued with method and effrontery, in which the commercial dynamic reproduces itself through feedback, since supply itself manufactures demand<1>p. 348</1>

The text starts from the premise that the common law does not operate as a static system, but as a tradition capable of developing new protective contours when material changes reconfigure interests worthy of protection. Here, the interest of the argument is methodological and does not depend on institutional transplant between common law and civil law, since the point lies not in specific techniques of precedent, but in the need to readjust legal categories when material transformation makes the available frame anachronistic.<1>p. 347</1>

Transposing this model to the IOC regime requires keeping the focus on the type of power described. The core of the problem lies not in isolated breaches, but in a private infrastructure of practical governance capable of organizing, at scale, conditions of participation and enjoyment.<1>p. 349</1>

The article's cautions also serve as a model, because privacy was designed as calibrated protection, limited by the public interest, by the institutional contexts in which information circulates by function and by proportionality to the means of propagation. It follows that limiting power does not depend on its public nature but on how it stabilizes and on the effects it produces on the conditions of life and participation. The relevant deficit is the lack of institutional reciprocity proportional to the dominion exercised over recognition, permanence and sanction, and it is in this strict sense that the platform occupies the place of the collectivity without authorization, that is, without submitting, in equivalent measure, to intelligible publicity of criteria, accessible reasoning, decisional coherence and effective avenues of contestation. The question is no longer whether the relationship is public or private but which instruments make this power examinable.

The prudence of the design proposed by Warren and Brandeis appears clearly in the section on limitations, in which the right to privacy is framed as calibrated protection, incapable of functioning as a general instrument of informational blocking.<1>p. 349</1>

The public interest functions as a limit, since protection does not extend to publications whose content is of public or general interest, so as to preserve the circulation of information relevant to the community and to prevent privacy from becoming censorship <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 16])</2>. Their work also sets limits by institutional context by recognizing that certain informational flows are part of the very functioning of institutions and, therefore, cannot be paralyzed by the new protection, as occurs with publications made in judicial bodies and in legislative bodies, as well as in equivalent communications <3>Brandeis</3><4>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 19])</4>. The delimitation is completed with a criterion of proportionality associated with the means of propagation, by admitting that, as a rule, there would be no redress for merely oral publication without special damage and that part of these occurrences must be tolerated to preserve freedom of expression<5>p. 349-350</5>

The methodological consequence of this calibration is that limiting power does not depend on its public nature, but on the way it stabilizes and on the effects it produces on conditions of life and participation. When practical normativity is exercised through mutable internal rules, through access architecture and through opaque informational intermediation, the relevant deficit is not the absence of a public-law label, but the absence of institutional reciprocity proportional to the dominion exercised over recognition, permanence and sanction.<1>p. 350</1>

It is in this strict sense that the expression “without authorization” operates as a descriptive category, since it names a power of social ordering that does not submit, in equivalent measure, to minimum requirements of intelligible publicity of criteria, accessible reasoning, decisional coherence and effective avenues of contestation compatible with the economic and identity relevance of what is at stake. From this point on, the task ceases to be discussing whether the relationship is private or public and becomes identifying which instruments of control make it possible to render examinable the rationality of the exercise of this power<1>p. 350</1>
Where does the Constitution place consumer protection?

The Constitution inscribes consumer protection on two planes. Article 5, item XXXII, of the Constitution<1><2>1</2></1> orders the State to promote it, as provided by law, and Article 170, items III, IV and V, of the Constitution<3><4>2</4></3> places it among the principles of an economic order founded on the valuing of human labor and on free enterprise and intended to ensure a dignified existence, alongside the social function of property and free competition. That is why consumer protection is an internal condition of the market's legitimacy and not a moralizing appendix. Free enterprise enters the same matrix, since Article 1, items III and IV, of the Constitution<5><6>3</6></5> links it to the dignity of the human person and to social values. Eros Roberto Grau reads consumer protection as a mandatory principle shaping economic activity and argues that free enterprise, free competition, the social function of property, consumer protection and the repression of abuse of economic power, which Article 173, paragraph 4, of the Constitution<7><8>4</8></7> provides for, shape one another.

Consumer protection does not enter the Brazilian constitutional order as a moralizing appendix of the market, but as one of its internal conditions of legitimacy. The Constitution inscribes it, on the one hand, on the plane of fundamental rights and, on the other, in the principled core of the economic order, which prevents its treatment as lateral protection, available at the supplier's convenience or subordinated to the private grammar of contract.<1>p. 504</1>

“Art. 5. All are equal before the law, without distinction of any nature, guaranteeing to Brazilians and to foreigners residing in the Country the inviolability of the right to life, to liberty, to equality, to security and to property, on the following terms: [...] XXXII - the State shall promote, as provided by law, the protection of the consumer” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]a)</2>.<3>p. 504</3>

“Art. 170. The economic order, founded on the valuing of human labor and on free enterprise, has the purpose of ensuring to all a dignified existence, in accordance with the dictates of social justice, observing the following principles: [...] III - social function of property; IV - free competition; V - consumer protection” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]a)</2>.<3>p. 504</3>

Consumer protection, in the constitutional text of 1988, is part of the very normative structure of the economic order, as a mandatory constitutional principle and a guideline shaping the functioning of economic activity.<1>p. 505</1>

Its normative meaning depends precisely on the articulated coexistence of free enterprise, free competition, social function of property, consumer protection and repression of abuse of economic power, principles that shape one another within the same constitutional matrix <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2010, p. 213)</2>.<3>p. 505-506</3>

§ 4 The law shall repress abuse of economic power aimed at the domination of markets, the elimination of competition and the arbitrary increase of profits” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]a)</2>.<3>p. 505</3>

The objectives in Article 3, items I and III, of the Constitution<1><2>5</2></1>, of building a free, just and solidary society and of reducing inequalities, rule out any constitutional neutrality in favor of private arrangements that deepen structural dependencies under the pretext of efficiency or innovation, and Bruno Miragem adds that consumer protection shapes the legitimate functioning of economic activity without depending on the supplier's tolerance. Property too is subject to its social function, under Article 5, item XXIII, of the Constitution<3><4>6</4></3>, and José Afonso da Silva shows that the social function bears on the very content of the right, its recognition and its guarantee, so that the social function is an internal element of legitimacy and not a peripheral correction. Fábio Konder Comparato shows that this containment is not an isolated innovation of recent constitutionalism, because the development of economic, social and cultural rights led to the recognition that private parties too have the duty to respect human rights. Governed enjoyment thus activates functional limits on private positions founded on exclusivity and technical control.
The Brazilian economic Constitution does not admit small private fiefdoms of unrestricted normative power.<1>p. 512</1>

“Art. 3. The fundamental objectives of the Federative Republic of Brazil are: I - to build a free, just and solidary society; [...] III - to eradicate poverty and marginalization and to reduce social and regional inequalities” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]a)</2>.<3>p. 506</3>

There is, therefore, no constitutional neutrality in favor of private arrangements that deepen structural dependencies under the pretext of efficiency, innovation or sectoral dynamism. In platform-governed markets, in which access, permanence, visibility and contestation of enjoyment come to be administered by technical-organizational design, the containment of private power ceases to be a peripheral theme and moves to the center of the problem. The Brazilian Constitution does not idolize private power merely because it is not state power; on the contrary, it provides express language to control it when it takes a structurally asymmetric form, especially because consumer protection shapes the legitimate functioning of economic activity and does not depend on the supplier's private tolerance <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 37)</2>.<3>p. 506</3>

Property is subject to its social function, and this functionalization does not act as a peripheral correction subsequent to the recognition of the right, but as an internal element of its very legitimacy.<1>p. 507</1>

The social function, in this key, bears on the very content of the right, on its recognition and on its guarantee, introducing into the internal structure of the legal position an interest that does not necessarily coincide with the isolated interest of the holder <1>Silva</1><2>(Silva, 2005, p. 283)</2>.<3>p. 507</3>

The constitutional containment of private economic power and the subordination of the exercise of property to socially justifiable purposes are not an isolated innovation of recent Brazilian constitutionalism, but an expression of a broader historical process of affirming the centrality of the human person against patrimonially absolutized forms of power. In this key, the evolution of human rights is not exhausted in negative liberties opposable to the State, since the very development of economic, social and cultural rights led to the recognition that, besides the Public Powers, individuals and legal entities of private law also have the duty to respect human rights of any kind <1>Comparato</1><2>(Comparato, 2015, p. 70)</2>.<3>p. 507</3>

It is not a matter of adding norms at random, but of recognizing that the governed enjoyment of the IOC activates, at the same time, constitutional requirements of limiting economic power, consumer-law duties of protecting vulnerability and functional limits on the exercise of private positions founded on exclusivity and technical control.<1>p. 503</1>
Why do terms of use and licenses not choose when the CDC applies?

Article 1 of the CDC<1><2>7</2></1> qualifies its norms as matters of public order and social interest, in execution of the constitutional commands, and so consumer public order enters the relationship before any clause, without terms of use or licenses choosing when it comes into play. The treatise by Benjamin, Marques and Bessa treats the CDC as a law of clearly constitutional origin, with norms that cannot be waived by contract, and Claudia Lima Marques and José Geraldo Brito Filomeno stress its mandatory nature. This public order blocks the global exclusion of the microsystem and its piecemeal sabotage, and Article 51, items IV, XI, XIII and XV, of the CDC<3><4>8</4></3> strikes down as null the iniquitous clauses, those that authorize unilateral cancellation or modification of the contract and those that contradict the protection system. On platforms, the precariousness of the bond is usually recycled as acceptance, and the system does not admit that structural vulnerability be disguised as consent sufficient to override legal protection.

Where the duty arises from the law, the consumer's adhesion is not enough to empty it <1>Denari · Benjamin +1</1><2>(Denari, 2011, p. 238; Benjamin, 2011, p. 494; Nery Jr., 2011, p. 577)</2>.<3>p. 509-510</3>

At the infraconstitutional level, this matrix finds direct concretization in the Consumer Protection Code, whose application does not depend on gracious recognition by the supplier. The CDC establishes consumer protection and defense norms of public order and social interest, precisely in execution of the constitutional commands that make consumer protection a fundamental right and a principle of the economic order. There is no room, then, for the fantasy that terms of use, digital licenses or predisposed contractual architectures might select when consumer public order will come into play.<1>p. 508</1>
Wherever there is a consumer relationship, consumer public order has already entered before any contractual clause.<1>p. 507</1>

The 1988 Constitution is the origin of the protective codification of the consumer in Brazil, so that the CDC receives a true constitutional guarantee, with superior hierarchy and public-order character, placing consumer protection among the structuring values of Brazilian private law, alongside — and in reciprocal containment with — free enterprise and private autonomy <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 72])</2>. This reading is reinforced when the work characterizes the CDC as a law of social function, a law of economic public order and a law of “clearly constitutional” origin, precisely to explain why its norms, although they apply to private relationships, are non-disposable and cannot be waived by contract <3>Bessa</3><4>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 115])</4>.<5>p. 508</5>

The mandatory nature of this regime is unequivocal: its norms cannot be waived by individual will and cannot be neutralized by contractual engineering designed to escape protective coverage <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 678; p. 804)</2> [...] That is why consumer public order cannot be treated as a negotiable legislative detail. It blocks both the global exclusion of the microsystem and its piecemeal sabotage, including through exoneration clauses, waiver of rights, unilateral cancellation, unilateral modification of contractual content and excessive advantages.<3>p. 508-509</3>

Article 1 of the CDC<1><2>7</2></1> qualifies its norms as matters of public order and social interest, which gives them a mandatory nature that cannot be overridden by the will of the parties <3>Filomeno</3><4>(Filomeno, 2011, p. 16)</4>.<5>p. 509</5>

“Contractual clauses relating to the supply of products and services that, among others: IV - establish obligations considered iniquitous, abusive [...]; XI - authorize the supplier to cancel the contract unilaterally, without the same right being granted to the consumer; [...] XIII - authorize the supplier to modify unilaterally the content or quality of the contract, after its conclusion; [...] XV - are in disagreement with the consumer protection system, are null and void by operation of law.<1>p. 509</1>

In a platform environment, this point is especially sensitive, because the precariousness of the bond is usually recycled as the user's “acceptance” of private regimes of mutability, opacity and sanction. The consumer system, however, does not admit that structural vulnerability be disguised as consent sufficient to override legal protection.<1>p. 509</1>

The point finds support in Zelmo Denari, Antonio Herman Benjamin, Nelson Nery Jr. and Miragem, and the application is not exhausted in the text of the Code either. Article 7 of the CDC<1><2>9</2></1> opens the microsystem to other sources, and Marques reads this opening as an updating interface, which integrates the rights ensured by external legislation, but not the limits to those rights, so that it reinforces protection and never serves as a privatist escape route. Article 47 of the CDC<3><4>10</4></3>, which orders clauses to be interpreted in the way most favorable to the consumer, already announces that unilaterally drafted ambiguities do not turn imposed precariousness into legal normality, and Article 4, items I, III and VI, of the CDC<5><6>11</6></5> and Article 6, items I, III, IV, VI and VIII, of the CDC<7><8>12</8></7> show a protection that bears on risk, opacity, deception, evidentiary asymmetry and unfair methods. On platforms, information, verifiability, permanence and contestation cannot be technical favors administered by whoever designs the environment. The regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption is not an extravagant construction, because a utility that depends on continuous governance, unilateral reconfiguration, technical opacity and asymmetric distribution of evidence is a constitutionally qualified case of containing asymmetries.

The rights recognized to the consumer and the duties imposed on the supplier cannot be validly suppressed, waived, limited or set aside by contract, terms of use, license or any other predisposed negotiated arrangement <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 380)</2>.<3>p. 506</3>

The protective regime being mandatory, no validity is lent to agreements that seek to empty the supplier's legal duties or to reduce, by contractual means, the intensity of the protection ensured to the consumer <1>Denari</1><2>(Denari, 2011, p. 238)</2>.<3>p. 510</3>

In consumer matters, individual will does not operate as a safe-conduct for the suppression of protective public order, especially when this would imply breaking the material balance of the relationship <1>Benjamin · Jr.</1><2>(Benjamin, 2011, p. 494; Nery Jr., 2011, p. 577)</2>.<3>p. 510</3>

The function of this opening, however, is not to relativize consumer protection, but to reinforce it. That is why the author observes that, in the CDC system, Art. 7 acts as an "updating interface", integrating into the microsystem the rights ensured by external legislation, "but not the limits to those rights" <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1120-1121)</2>.<3>p. 510</3>

The contractual interpretation most favorable to the consumer already announces, from the outset, that unilaterally drafted ambiguities cannot turn imposed precariousness into legal normality.<1>p. 511</1>

The constitutional centrality of the theme also appears clearly when one recalls that the National Consumer Relations Policy expressly recognizes the consumer's vulnerability, harmonization founded on good faith and balance, and the efficient curbing of abuses. The consumer's basic rights, in turn, include adequate and clear information, protection against misleading and abusive advertising, prevention and redress of damages, and facilitation of the defense of their rights. These provisions already show that consumer protection, in the constitutional order concretized by the CDC, is not limited to protecting the wallet against ostensive defects of a stable thing; it bears on risk, opacity, deception, evidentiary asymmetry and unfair methods of organizing the market.<1>p. 511</1>

On platforms, this means that information, verifiability, conditions of permanence and possibilities of contestation cannot be relegated to the status of technical favors administered by the very party that concentrates the design of the environment. Therefore, the constitutional matrix affirmed here does not authorize the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption to be treated as an extravagant construction or a theoretical deviation in search of a problem of its own.<1>p. 511</1>

When the utility consumed depends on continuous governance, unilateral reconfiguration, technical opacity and asymmetric distribution of the means of proof, the law is not facing an extrasystemic gray zone, but a constitutionally qualified case of containing structural asymmetries.<1>p. 511</1>
How do fundamental rights reach the platform's power without making it a State?

The horizontal effect of fundamental rights, that is, their application in relationships between private parties, gains concreteness when the relevant subjection comes from private centers of power capable of organizing access, permanence, visibility, reputation, evidence and contestation at scale. Daniel Sarmento argues that the Constitution radiates effects onto private bonds when the concentration of power becomes legally relevant, and Ingo Wolfgang Sarlet affirms that this binding does not presuppose turning the private party into a state entity. The criterion is the material density of the power and its effects on the other party, and, for Isadora Beatriz Magalhães Santos, the more unequal the relationship, the smaller the room for an absolutized reading of contractual autonomy. The platform remains a private party, but it does not thereby gain a constitutional license to operate as a small jurisdiction immune to control.

The private relationship remains private, but the fantasy disappears that this formal qualification, by itself, would make it immune to the normative force of fundamental rights <1>Sarlet</1><2>(Sarlet, 2018, p. 528-529)</2>.<3>p. 512-513</3>

In contexts like these, private autonomy cannot function as a screen to shield materially asymmetric arrangements, because the Constitution is not limited to containing public power, radiating effects also onto bonds between private parties when the concentration of power becomes legally relevant <1>Sarmento</1><2>(Sarmento, 2010, p. 51; p. 258; p. 285)</2>.<3>p. 512</3>

The application of fundamental rights to private relationships does not presuppose the artificial transformation of the private party into a state entity, but arises from the need to protect the person in the face of the power concretely exercised by another private party.<1>p. 513</1>
The legally relevant point lies in the material density of the power exercised and in the concrete effects it produces on the sphere of the other subject of the relationship.<1>p. 513</1>

The more unequal the private relationship, the smaller the legitimate room for an absolutized reading of contractual autonomy and the greater the need to protect the fundamental right affected <1>Santos</1><2>(Santos, 2019, p. 112; p. 132)</2>.<3>p. 514</3>
In simple terms: the platform remains a private party, but it does not thereby gain a constitutional license to operate as a small jurisdiction immune to control.<1>p. 516</1>

The clauses of the ecosystem studied make the phenomenon empirical. Under Riot Games' Terms of Service, the company may terminate or suspend accounts when it reasonably determines that this would be in the best interest of the community or the services, may keep the account suspended while it reviews the player's request, and the player may contest the decision, and it provides for bans, including hardware bans, content removal, progress resets and functional restrictions, regardless of whether the behavior is listed in the rules. The discipline reaches uses outside the match, such as streaming game content, and a penalty in one game may radiate to another. There is here a private center of governance in an integrated network, whose public relevance arises from the brute fact that it organizes, on a continuing basis, the consumer's practical position.

The very clauses of the ecosystem examined make this phenomenon too empirical to be treated as an abstraction. Riot reserves the power to terminate or suspend accounts based on criteria formulated by itself, including with regard to the “best interest” of its community or its services. It also provides for bans, suspension, account deletion, hardware bans, content removal, progress resets and functional restrictions, extends its discipline to off-platform uses linked to game content and radiates penalties from one service to another within the same ecosystem.<1>p. 514-515</1>

If you think we made a mistake, contact our Player Support team with the details here and we will review your case, although we may suspend your account during our review. Terminations and suspensions may be temporary or permanent, at our reasonable discretion. You may also contest our decisions (see Clause 16).<1>p. 515</1>

In case of violation, Riot reserves the right to take appropriate disciplinary measures, including temporary bans, suspension, or termination and deletion of the account, hardware bans, content removal, resets of user progress, limitations on chat functionality and restrictions and bans from matchmaking queues, in order to protect the integrity and spirit of the Riot Services, regardless of whether a specific behavior is listed or not in the User Rules as inappropriate.<1>p. 515</1>
We may take disciplinary measures against you for any use of the Riot Services, such as violating the User Rules while streaming Game Content.<1>p. 515</1>

We are not, therefore, facing a mere technical infrastructure of entertainment, but a private center of governance that disciplines permanence, history, visibility, progression and contestation in an integrated network. The public relevance of this power does not arise from a grandiloquent metaphor, but from the brute fact that it organizes, on a continuing basis, the consumer's practical position in the digital environment.<1>p. 515</1>

The constitutional frame brings together the promotion of the good of all without discrimination, in Article 3, item IV, of the Constitution<1><2>13</2></1>, and, in Article 5, items V, X, XXXV and LIV, of the Constitution<3><4>14</4></3>, compensation for material, moral or image damage, the inviolability of intimacy, private life, honor and image, access to the courts and due process. Exclusions, suspensions, reputational erasures and invasive monitoring are therefore not simple internal administration of the service, because they affect the consumer's biographical trajectory, informational integrity and capacity to respond. In the digital environment, power also runs through personal data. Canavez and coauthors treat data as legally relevant projections of personality, and Canavez, Santos and Mendes record that the case law of the STF confirmed autonomous fundamental rights to the protection of personal data and to informational self-determination.

The promotion of the good of all without discrimination, the protection of honor, image and the personal sphere, the inviolability of intimacy, private life, honor and image, access to the courts and the prohibition of deprivation of property without due process make up, here, a decisive constitutional frame.<1>p. 516</1>

In platform environments, exclusions, suspensions, removals, reputational erasures and invasive monitoring cannot be treated as technical noise or simple “internal administration of the service”, because they affect the consumer's biographical trajectory, informational integrity, practical permanence in the ecosystem and very capacity to respond to the power that governs them. The problem is not only patrimonial; it is also one of personality, of practical freedom and of the controllability of private power.<1>p. 516-517</1>

Data are not neutral matter of market circulation, but legally relevant projections of personality, whose protection is linked to human dignity and informational self-determination <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 155-156)</2>.<3>p. 517</3>

The reinforced legal containment of digitally mediated private powers does not arise from theoretical voluntarism, but from the finding that the information society and private surveillance structures imposed the recognition and explicit statement of new fundamental rights, especially the protection of personal data and informational self-determination. Along these lines, the development of information and communication technologies, in a surveillance society marked by the mitigation of privacy, imposed the need to reflect on new fundamental rights <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 69-70)</2>. The same key is reinforced when one recognizes that the economic exploitation of personal data without sufficient consent did not remain only at the infraconstitutional level, the case law of the STF having confirmed the existence of autonomous fundamental rights to the protection of personal data and to informational self-determination <3>Mendes</3><4>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 82-83)</4>.<5>p. 517</5>
Why does the horizontal effect need the CDC to operate?

The horizontal effect is indispensable but not enough as an operational grammar, because the law of the platform may also govern perception, predictability, exposure and self-determination, and a dogmatic language is needed that reaches architecture, practices, information, sanction and evidence. Consumer law comes in here as a normative infrastructure of containment and not as a sectoral appendix. Bruno Miragem explains that vulnerability before a supplier in a dominant position justifies the CDC's norms limiting private power and that good faith is the central brake on that superiority, and Claudia Lima Marques defines abusiveness as an imbalance of rights and obligations and assigns objective good faith a limiting function over conduct and clauses. Miragem also recalls that Articles 39 and 51 of the CDC<1><2>15</2></1> equalize a factually unequal relationship, and this grammar is enough to bring the containment of the platform down to the ground of the CDC.
The platform may shape its service, but not turn that shaping into private sovereignty over the user's position.<1>p. 519</1>

The Lex Plataformae does not govern only access and use; it may also govern the user's perception, predictability, exposure and margins of self-determination. All of this explains why the horizontal effect of fundamental rights, although indispensable, is still not enough on its own as an operational grammar of the problem. It is necessary to bring this constitutional containment back into a dogmatic language of control capable of touching, concretely, architecture, practices, information, sanction and evidence regimes. It is here that consumer law comes in not as a sectoral appendix, but as a normative infrastructure for containing the asymmetries produced by the Lex Plataformae.<1>p. 518</1>

Because of the consumer's vulnerability before the supplier, who holds a dominant position in the contract, the CDC establishes a series of norms limiting the supplier's private power, through clear state legislative intervention in contractual autonomy, aimed at protecting the interests of the vulnerable party <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 274)</2>. This reading gains density when one recognizes that, in contemporary society, the consumer relationship presents itself less as an expression of contractual freedom and more as the fulfillment of a need to consume. In this context, the notion of abuse expresses the prevalence of the supplier's dominant position over the consumer's vulnerability, good faith being the central legal brake on the exercise of this bargaining superiority <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, p. 324)</4>.<5>p. 519</5>

Convergently, Marques defines abusiveness as an "imbalance or mismatch of rights and obligations between the parties", associated with the authorization of conduct contrary to good faith and with the abuse of the preponderant contractual position <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 162)</2>.<3>p. 514</3>

In contexts of informational asymmetry, practical dependence and unilateral predisposition of the rules of the bond, consumer protection requires that the exercise of contractual powers be subject to parameters of loyalty, reasonableness, economic-social purpose and respect for the trust legitimately placed in the relationship. This is exactly the point developed by Marques when she states that "the notion of objective good faith, as a new principle guiding the conduct of the contracting parties in captive contracts, means a new and important limitation on the exercise of subjective rights", so that the exercise of the right will be abusive when diverted from its economic-social function or exercised in disloyal circumstances <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 111)</2>. The author adds that good faith has a limiting function, "reducing the freedom of action of the contractual partners" and controlling abusive conduct and clauses <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 221)</4>.<5>p. 519</5>

Arts. 39 and 51 make up protection mechanisms intended precisely to equalize a factually unequal relationship, typifying abusive practices and sanctioning abusive clauses with nullity by operation of law, in clear mitigation of pacta sunt servanda <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 741)</2>.<3>p. 519</3>

In practical terms, the containment of the platform need not be built only through lofty constitutional mediation: good faith, abuse of dominant position, excessive disadvantage and nullity of abusive clauses already offer sufficient grammar to bring it down to the ground of the CDC.<1>p. 519-520</1>

The doors appear in the provisions. Article 14 of the CDC<1><2>16</2></1> holds the service supplier liable for defects in the service and for insufficient information about enjoyment and risks, Article 20 of the CDC<3><4>17</4></3> reaches quality defects that make the service unfit or reduce its value, and Article 39, items IV, V and XII, of the CDC<5><6>18</6></5> prohibits taking advantage of the consumer's weakness or ignorance, demanding a manifestly excessive advantage and failing to set a time limit for the obligation or leaving its starting date to the supplier's sole discretion. Through these doors, the problem can already be grasped as defect, inadequacy, abuse, exploitation of vulnerability and unilateral manipulation of the conditions of enjoyment, and the focus shifts from isolated clauses to structural patterns of governance, verifiability and reasoning. The platform's public relevance does not turn it into a State, but it prevents its governance from being read as an internal business detail, and control needs to reach the architecture of the relationship.

Strict liability for defects in the service and for insufficient or inadequate information, the discipline of quality defects that make the service unfit or reduce its value and the prohibition of abusive practices that take advantage of the consumer's weakness, impose excessive advantage or leave performance of the obligation to the supplier's sole discretion show that the problem of the Lex Plataformae need not be framed only as a lofty conflict between Constitution and market. It can already be grasped, operationally, as defect, inadequacy, abuse, exploitation of vulnerability and unilateral manipulation of the conditions of enjoyment. This shifts the focus from isolated clauses to structural patterns of governance, verifiability and reasoning.<1>p. 520</1>

The public relevance of the powers of the Lex Plataformae does not authorize confusing platform with State, but it prevents its governance from being read as an internal business detail, legally neutral. When a private supplier organizes, by design and enforcement, the conditions of access, permanence, equivalence, visibility, sanction and contestation of a continuous consumption experience, legal control cannot remain a prisoner of the contractual surface. It needs to reach the architecture of the relationship and reintroduce, within it, criteria of controllability, reasoning and verifiability. Without this, opacity, unilateral mutation and systematic difficulties of contestation cease to appear as pathologies and come to be naturalized as the ordinary condition of digital consumption.<1>p. 520</1>
What does Vanguard show when governance reaches the consumer's computer?

The case that puts the construction to the test is Vanguard, Riot Games' anti-cheat program. According to the company's official communications, it consists of a client and a kernel-mode driver, that is, a low-level component installed in the deepest and most privileged layer of the operating system, and it starts at boot, when the computer starts up. In League of Legends it must remain active whenever the client is open, and disabling it prevents play. The Terms of Service allow monitoring use on the user's computer and running the software in the background, and an official update at the end of 2025 extended the concern to the initial stages of hardware startup, with VALORANT possibly blocked until the user updates the firmware, the basic software of the motherboard, or enables required security layers. The protection of the object becomes preventive and continuing governance, which reaches the machine before the decision to enjoy.
What is at stake is the redefinition of the material boundaries of the user's sovereignty over their own equipment.<1>p. 521</1>

The case of the Vanguard anti-cheat exposes, in a particularly clear way, a qualitative mutation in the private governance of the immaterial object of consumption. It is no longer only a matter of conditioning the enjoyment of the game on internal rules of conduct, progression or permanence in the ecosystem, but of projecting the requirements of competitive integrity onto the consumer's own material infrastructure.<1>p. 520-521</1>

In the official support communications devoted to League of Legends and VALORANT, Riot itself describes Vanguard as security software composed of a client active while the game is running and a kernel-mode driver, that is, installed in the deepest and most privileged layer of the operating system, with access far greater than that of ordinary applications <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024r; Riot Games, 2024t)</2>.<3>p. 521</3>

In the case of League of Legends, Riot makes explicit that Vanguard must remain active not only during the match, but also whenever the client is open, and that its deactivation, uninstallation or unauthorized interaction prevents use of the game; in the case of VALORANT, it further states that deactivating the system requires restarting the machine to restore the possibility of playing <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024r; Riot Games, 2024t)</2>.<3>p. 521</3>

In an official update published at the end of 2025, Riot makes even more explicit the logic of preventive governance that sustains Vanguard. The text states that the company identified a critical flaw in several modern motherboards, capable of allowing the invisible injection of code in the very initial stages of the machine's startup, even before the operating system has fully loaded. On the basis of this finding, Riot justifies the hardening of its integrity requirements by arguing that components loaded earlier in the boot process operate with a higher degree of privilege and, precisely for that reason, can compromise the entire environment before the operating system or the anti-cheat itself can react. The document also clarifies that, given this breach, Vanguard's restriction service may prevent VALORANT from running until the user updates the motherboard firmware or enables certain security layers deemed necessary by the platform.<1>p. 522</1>

Riot contractually admits the possibility of actively monitoring the use of its services not only on its own servers, but also on the consumer's computer or device, and provides that the anti-cheat software may remain running in the background on the device. With this, the protection of the IOC does not remain confined to the concrete moment of the match. It becomes a vector of preventive and continuing governance over the technical environment in which the game will run, reaching the machine even before the specific decision to enjoy.<1>p. 521-522</1>

The technical documents show the practical reach. Riot admits that Vanguard may block third-party applications and require changes to BIOS or UEFI, the basic interfaces that prepare the machine to start the operating system, and impose TPM 2.0, an integrity verification module, Secure Boot, which prevents untrusted components from starting, IOMMU, which isolates device access to memory, and memory integrity, and it recognizes that incorrect changes to these settings may cause serious problems on the computer. It may also prevent play when it identifies low-level drivers, such as those of outdated monitoring tools and lighting control. The platform conditions the enjoyment of the immaterial object on the machine's prior conformity with private standards of integrity and compatibility unilaterally defined by it.
The user's computer comes, functionally, to be administered as an extension of the game's competitive environment.<1>p. 527</1>

Riot itself, in documents aimed at developers and users of VALORANT, admits that Vanguard may block third-party applications, require sensitive changes to BIOS or UEFI, impose enabling of TPM 2.0, Secure Boot, IOMMU, memory integrity and other security layers, besides recognizing that incorrect changes to these settings may cause serious problems on the computer.<1>p. 526-527</1>

These are the acronyms for Basic Input/Output System and Unified Extensible Firmware Interface. They designate the basic software interfaces that reside in the hardware and are responsible for preparing the machine to start the operating system.<1>p. 527</1>

On the system restrictions page, Riot expressly admits that it may limit access to the games when it identifies machines considered excessively prone to cheating, including because of outdated versions of Windows or specific equipment configurations, requiring the user to make sensitive changes to BIOS or UEFI, that is, to the machine's basic startup systems, with enabling of features such as TPM 2.0 (a security module used for integrity verification and protected key storage), Secure Boot (a mechanism that prevents untrusted components from starting), IOMMU (a technology that isolates device access to memory) and memory integrity mechanisms, as well as updates to the BIOS and to the operating system itself <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025q)</2>.<3>p. 527</3>

Even more concretely, the guidance on incompatible software clarifies that Vanguard may prevent VALORANT from running when it identifies “.sys” files, that is, low-level drivers responsible for communication between the operating system and functions or components of the computer, instructing the user to remove the related software or even to manually delete the blocked file; among the examples mentioned by Riot itself are old drivers, outdated monitoring tools and RGB lighting control programs<1>p. 527</1>

The platform conditions the enjoyment of the immaterial object on the prior conformity of the machine's technical ecosystem with private standards of integrity and compatibility unilaterally defined by it.<1>p. 527</1>

Clause 10.2 of the Terms completes the design, because it allows Riot to alter, update, nerf, which is the adjustment that reduces the power or usefulness of a feature, or restrict features and Virtual Products, to require the installation of software at any time and to assign to the user, and not to Riot, the purchase of the additional software or hardware that the new specifications require. The Terms also seek to limit the company's liability. It is here that the case ceases to be only a discussion about fighting cheating and becomes a classic problem of the supplier's contractual shielding in the face of an invasive technical architecture that it itself imposes.

In an effort to constantly improve the Riot Services, promote the evolution of our games and keep the Riot Services safe, fun and protected, you agree that we may alter, modify, update, suspend, “nerf” or restrict your access to any features or parts of the Riot Services, including Virtual Products (for example, we may alter some features of Virtual Products for regulatory or legal reasons or to improve the game experience) and we may require you to download and install software and updates of any software necessary to support the Riot Services, at any time, without liability to you, to the extent permitted by law.<1>p. 526</1>

You also understand and agree that these changes or updates to the Riot Services may change the system specifications needed to play our games and, in that case, you, and not Riot Games, will be responsible for purchasing any additional software or hardware needed to access and play our games.<1>p. 526</1>

In parallel, the contractual wording seeks to reduce the supplier's patrimonial exposure by stating that the services are offered as is, without broad warranties, assigning to the user responsibility for use and limiting Riot's liability for losses and damages, including in relation to failures linked to not installing updates or to maintaining minimum system requirements.<1>p. 526</1>

The general contractual frame thus seeks to frame in advance the submission of the consumer's equipment to additional layers of surveillance, compulsory adaptation and shifting of risk. This is the point at which the case ceases to be only a discussion about fighting cheating and becomes a classic problem of the supplier's contractual shielding in the face of an invasive technical architecture that it itself imposes.<1>p. 526</1>
Why does the security argument not settle the question?

Under the vocabulary of security, the expansion appears as technical inevitability, but this discourse does not by itself neutralize the legal relevance of the architecture. Canavez, Santos and Mendes show that the security argument can legitimize the expansion of private powers when the demand for data is normalized by routine acceptances, Mariana Monteiro da Costa argues that monitoring technologies embody human choices and restructure power relations, and Danilo Doneda shows that, when organized data function as operational substitutes for the person, surveillance becomes a potential mechanism for affecting their autonomy. The problem becomes one of proportionality, necessity, transparency and justifiability of the technical interference, and the constitutional filter still stands, because, with Sarlet, fundamental rights radiate over the entire legal order, and the platform acts on the consumer's equipment, privacy and real possibility of enjoyment.

Under the vocabulary of security, this expansion usually appears as if it were simple technical inevitability. But the discourse of security does not, by itself, neutralize the legal relevance of the architecture adopted.<1>p. 522</1>

In the digital environment, storage, sharing and persistent monitoring of information represent a threat to privacy serious enough to require specific normative containment, especially in a surveillance society in which data processing becomes a central asset of business models and of behavioral control <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 69; p. 73; p. 82)</2>. The security argument itself can function as a legitimizer of the expansion of private powers over fundamental spheres of informational life, especially when the demand for data and structural surveillance are normalized by routine and barely intelligible acceptances<3>p. 522-523</3>

It is not enough, therefore, to invoke fighting cheating as a magic word. The problem becomes one of proportionality, necessity, transparency and justifiability of the degree of technical interference demanded of the consumer.<1>p. 523</1>

Monitoring technologies and algorithmic governance embody human choices and restructure power relations over the user, allowing veiled control and the favoring of their own interests by those who dominate the digital infrastructure<1>p. 523</1>

When organized data function as operational substitutes for the person, surveillance ceases to be a simple administrative instrument and becomes a potential mechanism for affecting individuality, autonomy and the free development of personality<1>p. 524-525</1>

Even if the agent remains private, the intensification of control over hardware, informational flows and practical conditions of use remains subject to the protective filter that radiates from the Constitution over the entire legal order <1>Sarlet</1><2>(Sarlet, 2018, p. 205; p. 531)</2>. The constitutional order remains in the room precisely because the platform does not act only on an abstract thing, but on the consumer's practical sphere, their equipment, their privacy and their real possibility of enjoying or not enjoying the object without subjecting the rest of the machine to mutable private standards of integrity.<3>p. 525-526</3>

The parameters of containment come from the CDC and the LGPD. Articles 8, 10 and 12 of the CDC<1><2>19</2></1> limit risks to those that are normal and foreseeable, prohibit the product that the supplier knows or should know to have a high degree of harmfulness or dangerousness and, in limit cases, reopen the door to treating invasive software as a defective or inadequately informed product. Article 6, items I, III and VI, of Law 13,709/2018<3><4>20</4></3>, the General Data Protection Law (LGPD), requires a specific and informed purpose, necessity and transparency, subject to commercial and industrial secrets, and Articles 7, 8 and 46 of Law 13,709/2018<5><6>21</6></5> call for an adequate legal basis, consent that is not automatically satisfied by ritualized acceptances and security measures capable of protecting the data. The platform cannot invoke security as an all-encompassing justification while maintaining opacity about the scope, the necessity and the agents of the processing.
Alleged security does not replace legally demonstrated security.<1>p. 533</1>

Products and services placed on the market cannot entail risks to health or safety beyond those that are normal and foreseeable given their nature and enjoyment, and the supplier cannot place into circulation a product or service that it knows or should know to present a high degree of harmfulness or dangerousness. In limit cases, liability itself for design defects or for insufficient or inadequate information about use and risks reopens the door to treating invasive software as a defective or inadequately informed product.<1>p. 532-533</1>

The data processing linked to Vanguard cannot be justified en bloc under the generic heading of “security”, because it must observe a legitimate, specific, explicit and informed purpose, necessity, with limitation to the indispensable minimum, and transparency, with clear, precise and accessible information. It also requires an adequate legal basis, is not automatically satisfied by ritualized and generic acceptances, and presupposes technical and administrative measures capable of effectively protecting the data. In other words, the platform cannot invoke security as an all-encompassing justification while maintaining opacity about the scope, necessity and agents of the processing.<1>p. 533</1>

“Art. 6 [...] VI - transparency: guarantee, to data subjects, of clear, precise and easily accessible information about the carrying out of the processing and the respective processing agents, subject to commercial and industrial secrets;” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2026]a)</2>.<3>p. 533</3>

What weight does the evidence in the case carry and what weighs on the other side?

Each source has its own weight. The central facts come from the supplier's own institutional voice, in the terms and the technical documents, and the press coverage by Wilde, Walker and Hill, from 2020, shows that the criticism of the always-on character did not arise as marginal paranoia, without by itself proving any expert conclusion. The reports on the Microsoft Q&A technical forum associate blue screens and crashes with Vanguard's technical ecosystem, but in one of them the technical answer does not attribute conclusive causality and mentions competing hypotheses, and the Reddit reports, about conflicts with hardware programs, study routines and debugging tools, have only illustrative value. Bricking, which is the functional disabling of the equipment, appears in a report that does not prove causality and serves as the limit form of the problem, not necessarily the most frequent. The argument does not depend on universal harm, and it is enough to show that the required architecture transfers to the consumer a legally relevant systemic risk.

Taken together, the sources are empirically valuable because they show, in the supplier's own institutional voice and in more than one game ecosystem, that the competitive protection of the IOC is implemented through deep technical access, early loading and structural permanence in the consumer's computing environment [...]<1>p. 521</1>

In specialized press coverage, the controversy revolved around the always-on character of the anti-cheat, kernel-level loading from system startup, the fear of persistent surveillance and interference with non-game uses of the equipment. It is the limit form of the problem. Not the only one, nor necessarily the most frequent, but the one that makes it impossible to pretend that we are only talking about “just another piece of game software”.<1>p. 532</1>
The argument does not depend on absolute demonstration of universal harm; it is enough to show that the required architecture transfers to the consumer a legally relevant systemic risk.<1>p. 530</1>

The most important point is comparative, because the always-on, kernel-resident architecture does not appear as an inevitable fact of every anti-cheat but as a choice that intensifies intrusion, dependence and risk. The comparison with Easy Anti-Cheat, another anti-cheat system, and the record that Vanguard's recent trajectory would indicate a reduction of its permanent residence in the kernel, with part of the detection shifted to user mode, the ordinary and less privileged space in which programs run, rest on a single source, a text on the Medium portal signed by the user Uoiyouiyouiy, and not on a communication from the company. On the other side, Rigney argues that fighting cheating is an asymmetric and escalating contest, a community text signed as SerTenseal seeks to separate relevant criticisms from exaggerations without denying crashes and loss of compatibility, and Riot states that user mode would be insufficient and that the driver does not collect or transmit data on its own. The interest in competitive integrity is legitimate, and the counterpoint confirms that the dispute is about the justifiability of the costs and not about their existence. The question is whether this interest is enough to authorize, without reinforced control, the expansion of technical power over the equipment.

The most important point here is comparative: the kernel-level always-on architecture does not appear as an inevitable fact of every anti-cheat, but as a technical choice that intensifies the degree of intrusion, dependence and risk assumed by the consumer in the name of the ecosystem's competitive integrity.<1>p. 529</1>

In a comparative text published on the Medium portal, the user Uoiyouiyouiy <1>(2026)</1> contrasts Vanguard with Easy Anti-Cheat to argue that the architecture adopted by Riot has historically been deeper and more aggressive, above all because of the loading of the driver at kernel level right at system startup and its permanence as a privileged observation layer of the machine.<2>p. 527</2>

The text is also particularly relevant in recording that, after the accumulated controversies around deep access, potential failures and systemic costs of this model, Vanguard's own recent trajectory would indicate a movement to reduce its permanent residence in the kernel and to shift part of the detection layers to user mode (that is, to the ordinary space in which programs run, less privileged and less risky than the kernel)<1>p. 528</1>

Nor would it be honest to fail to recognize that there exists, even among the harshest criticisms, a consistent technical-cultural discourse in defense of more invasive measures, according to which fighting cheats in competitive games involves an asymmetric contest and continuous escalation, which would make understandable the adoption of deep countermeasures by the platform. This counterpoint is useful because it prevents an easy caricature of the practice. The serious legal question was never whether there is a legitimate interest in preserving competitive integrity; of course there is. The question is another: whether this interest is enough to authorize, without reinforced control, the expansion of the supplier's technical power over the material base of the consumer's equipment.<1>p. 532</1>

As a counterpoint to the more critical readings of the case, there also circulates a technical-cultural discourse according to which public resistance to Vanguard stems, at least in part, from insufficient understanding of the structural dynamics of fighting cheats in competitive games, marked by an asymmetric contest and by continuous escalation of cheating techniques ever deeper in the system, which is why more invasive measures would be presented as a functionally justifiable cost of preserving competitive integrity <1>Rigney</1><2>(Rigney, 2024)</2>.<3>p. 532</3>

[...] the very community text that seeks to correct “misinformation” does not eliminate the central objections, recognizing as real problems the possibility of crashing or disabling computers, the restriction on customizations and the loss of compatibility with part of the user base, especially on Linux<1>p. 532</1>

In an institutional statement prepared by its security and privacy teams, Riot builds an explicit defense of Vanguard's invasive architecture against public criticism about privacy and security. The text seeks to justify kernel-level access on the argument that more sophisticated cheats no longer operate only in the ordinary space of software, but advance into deeper layers of the operating system; therefore, according to the company, an anti-cheat restricted to user mode would be technically insufficient to preserve so-called competitive integrity.<1>p. 522</1>

At the same time, the communication tries to reduce the perception of risk by maintaining that the driver does not, by itself, collect or transmit information from the user's computer and by highlighting internal and external security reviews, as well as a bounty program for identifying vulnerabilities.<1>p. 522</1>
