What does the Legal Framework for Electronic Games recognize?

Sectoral regulation dismantles two simplifications, that the sector would be legally invisible and that it would be enough to name it in a statute to resolve the conflicts of its governance. Articles 1, 2 and 5 of Law 14,852/2024<1><2>22</2></1> create the legal framework for the electronic games industry, regulate its economic chain and define electronic game, and Articles 11 and 12 of Law 14,852/2024<3><4>23</4></3> treat the sector as innovation and culture. The recognition reinforces that games operated as a service are ecosystems of continuous operation, and it coexists with recurring concerns about vulnerable audiences, microtransactions, random mechanisms, personal data and integrated advertising, which are typical effects of these ecosystems and not accidents.
The recognition, however, does not eliminate the legal tensions, it only tends to make them more predictable.<1>p. 493</1>

The sectoral regulation of electronic games matters, above all, because it dismantles two bad simplifications: that the sector would be legally invisible and that it would be enough to name it legislatively to resolve the central conflicts of its governance.<1>p. 543</1>

The legal framework for electronic games expressly recognizes the existence of an industry of its own, regulates its central economic chain — manufacturing, importation, commercialization, development and commercial use — and provides a normative definition of what counts as an electronic game, including interactive audiovisual works developed as a computer program, devices and accessories, and software consumed by download or streaming.<1>p. 543</1>

“Art. 11. [...] investment in the development of electronic games is considered investment in research, development, innovation and culture. Art. 12. The development of electronic games is considered a cultural segment for the purposes of Law No. 8,313/1991.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2024]b)</2>.<3>p. 544</3>

The institutionalization of the sector matters because it reinforces, documentarily, the reading that games (above all under models operated as a service) are not limited to isolated products delivered in a single event. The offer is realized as an ecosystem sustained by continuous operation, permanent updating and enforcement of internal rules that are part of the material content of the supply.<1>p. 493</1>

What matters is to record the minimum context in which games operated as a service come to concentrate public and legal attention, highlighting vectors that reappear when enjoyment depends on an environment of continuous operation with intense private governance. Against this background, a double movement is observed. On one side, there is an effort to institutionalize games as a relevant economic and cultural activity. On the other, there is a recurrence of concerns linked to the protection of vulnerable audiences, to monetization through microtransactions and random mechanisms, to the processing of personal data and to market and advertising practices integrated into the very experience of enjoyment.<1>p. 493</1>

The recognition of the sector as a relevant economic and cultural activity coexists with predictable focal points linked to the protection of children and adolescents, to monetization through microtransactions and random mechanisms, to the processing of personal data and to market and advertising practices integrated into the environment of enjoyment. These vectors do not appear as episodic accidents, but as typical effects of ecosystems in which utility is realized over time, under private governance of the environment and through rules susceptible to unilateral modulation, with structural asymmetries of intelligibility and agency.<1>p. 496</1>

The recognition comes in a key of regulated economic freedom. Article 3 of Law 14,852/2024<1><2>24</2></1> declares the activity free, subject to Article 173 of the Constitution<3><4>25</4></3>, and orders that the age rating take into account the risks of microtransactions, the purchases that, in games as a service, tend to occur continuously and in segments within enjoyment itself. Article 6, items IV, V, VI and VII, of Law 14,852/2024<5><6>26</6></5> places among the principles fundamental rights, consumer protection, the full protection of children and adolescents and data protection, which prevents any legal infantilization of the problem. The sole paragraph of Article 5 of Law 14,852/2024<7><8>27</8></7> excludes from the definition of electronic game games involving betting or with a random or forecast-based outcome, and nothing follows from this about loot boxes. The framework also inserted the registration of games into Article 2, item VI, of Law 9,279/1996<9><10>28</10></9>, the Industrial Property Law, which makes it even more necessary to contain the proprietarian temptation to capture conflicts that, on the plane of enjoyment, remain conflicts of governed consumption.

The law affirms the freedom of manufacturing, importation, commercialization, development and commercial use of electronic games, but does so under express reference to Art. 173 of the Constitution<1><2>25</2></1> and to current legislation. This is relevant because the framework does not enshrine a sectoral free-for-all disguised as friendly modernity.<3>p. 544</3>

“Art. 3 The manufacturing, importation, commercialization, development and commercial use of electronic games are free, subject to the provisions of Art. 173 of the Federal Constitution<1><2>29</2></1> and of current legislation. § 1 The State shall carry out the indicative age rating, prior state authorization being waived for the development and exploitation of the electronic games covered by this Law. § 2 In carrying out the indicative age rating of electronic games, the risks related to the use of microtransaction mechanisms shall be taken into account.” <3>Brasil</3><4>(Brasil, [2024]b)</4>.<5>p. 544</5>
In games as a service, acquisition tends to occur continuously and in segments, inserted into the very experience of enjoyment.<1>p. 494</1>

The framework organizes the sector institutionally through principles and guidelines and, in its core most important for this thesis, affirms that electronic games must be conceived in light of respect for fundamental rights and democratic values, consumer protection, the full protection of children and adolescents, and the preservation of privacy, the protection of personal data and informational self-determination. The perspective is decisive in showing that the legal order already treats the sector as an economic and cultural activity crossed by multisectoral public concerns, and not as a playful enclave left solely to private enterprise. The dogmatic relevance of this lies in preventing any attempt at legal infantilization of the problem, as if electronic games still belonged to the regulatory limbo of “it's just entertainment”.<1>p. 544-545</1>

Sole paragraph. Commercial promotions or lottery modalities regulated by Laws No. 13,756, of December 12, 2018, and 14,790, of December 29, 2023, or any type of game that offers some type of bet, with prizes in real or virtual assets, or that involves a random or forecast-based outcome, are not considered electronic games, the companies and professionals involved in the production or distribution of these activities being prohibited from benefiting from any advantage defined in this Law.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2024]b)</2>.<3>p. 544</3>

“Art. 2 The protection of rights relating to industrial property [...] is effected through: […] VI - granting of registration for electronic games.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2024]c)</2>.<3>p. 547</3>

The amendment made by the legal framework in inserting the granting of registration for electronic games into the Industrial Property Law shows that games have come to be considered, more robustly, as an object of legal protection within the innovation economy. This has value for the thesis because it confirms that the sector was assimilated by the legal order not only as a cultural and market activity, but also as a reality capable of radiating consequences into the regimes of exclusivity. The consequence, however, is not to turn intellectual property into the total language of the problem. On the contrary, it makes even more necessary the containment of the proprietarian temptation to capture entirely conflicts that, on the plane of enjoyment, remain conflicts of governed consumption.<1>p. 547</1>
Where do loot boxes appear and what does the Digital Statute prohibit?

Loot boxes, mechanisms for obtaining random items upon payment, appear by name in the preliminary reading of the sector and in sectoral regulation. In them, utility and value depend on internal regimes of distribution, availability and rarity defined by the platform, linked to scarcity and time windows that make decisions dependent on anticipation, urgency and expectation. The institutional attention paid to them does not stem from moralizing the sector but from the fact that the supplier concentrates the criteria on availability, rotation, rarity and, where applicable, probability, with low external reconstructibility. Under the IOC regime, these mechanisms condense instituted rarity, anticipation, criterial opacity and unilateral modulation, with effects that may appear as erosion of utility and reconfiguration of value even when access is formally available. The protection of children and adolescents comes in because, in games operated as a service, consumption decisions tend to fragment over time, mediated by cycles of return, urgency, promises of progression and social comparison, and the focus on minors makes visible asymmetries of understanding and contestation.

The point of greatest sensitivity appears when monetization relies on random mechanisms for obtaining items, often treated in public debate as loot boxes. In these cases, the utility and value of what is acquired come to depend on internal regimes of distribution, on availability criteria and on limits defined by the platform, besides being linked to signals of scarcity, time windows and rarity regimes that make decisions more dependent on anticipation, urgency and expectation. Institutional discussion then tends to concentrate on minimum transparency of the conditions of acquisition, protection of vulnerable audiences and control of practices that induce consumption, not by moralizing the sector, but because the supplier concentrates internal criteria on availability, rotation, rarity and, where applicable, probability, under conditions of low external reconstructibility.<1>p. 494-495</1>

In this context, Law No. 15,211/2025 <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]c)</2> offers sufficient normative anchoring to situate the focal point by regulating, from the standpoint of protecting children and adolescents, the functionality of loot boxes as a mechanism for random acquisition upon payment. The interest of the statute, here, is evidential. Certain mechanics of the ecosystem have already been identified as structurally sensitive and, therefore, open to treatment by criteria. Under the IOC regime, such mechanisms condense elements such as instituted rarity, anticipation, criterial opacity and unilateral modulation, with effects that may manifest as material erosion of utility and reconfiguration of value, even if access remains formally available.<3>p. 495</3>

The protection of children and adolescents is one of these recurring vectors. Its centrality does not derive only from concerns about content, but from the combination of interactivity, permanence of the bond and exposure to acquisition and retention mechanisms built into the interfaces and rules of the environment. In games operated as a service, consumption decisions tend to be fragmented over time, mediated by cycles of return, signals of urgency, promises of progression, social comparison and incentives embedded in the very design of enjoyment. The focus on minors thus functions as an institutional trigger to make visible asymmetries of understanding and of capacity to contest in environments governed by architecture.<1>p. 494</1>

Law 15,211/2025, the Digital Statute of Children and Adolescents, has evidential interest, because it shows that these mechanics have already been identified as structurally sensitive. Article 5 of Law 15,211/2025<1><2>30</2></1> imposes duties of prevention, protection, information and security according to the best interest, Article 20 of Law 15,211/2025<3><4>31</4></3> prohibits loot boxes in games directed at children and adolescents, and also in those likely to be accessed by this audience, and Article 22 of Law 15,211/2025<5><6>32</6></5> prohibits profiling for commercial advertising. The regime is not lax, since Articles 29 and 40 of Law 15,211/2025<7><8>33</8></7> require the removal of content that violates rights and a legal representative in the country, and Articles 1 to 3 of Decree 12,622/2025<9><10>34</10></9> make the National Data Protection Agency the administrative authority and provide for blocking orders. Its entry into force was brought forward to March 2026, and this reveals a concrete regulatory problem and not a symbolic agenda.
Sectoral normativity, therefore, already sees the games market as a place of sensitive monetization, behavioral shaping and informational vulnerability.<1>p. 545</1>
BRASIL. Lei nº 15.211, de 17 de setembro de 2025. Dispõe sobre a proteção de crianças e adolescentes em ambientes digitais (Estatuto Digital da Criança e do Adolescente).<1>p. 806</1>

The Digital Statute of Children and Adolescents reinforces this diagnosis by making explicit, on another normative front, that the digital environment is not neutral and that suppliers are subject to positive duties of prevention, protection, information and security. The very material content of the best interest of the child and adolescent, in this context, already covers privacy, security, mental and physical health, access to information, freedom to participate in society and well-being. The norm goes beyond programmatic discourse by prohibiting loot boxes in games directed at children and adolescents and banning profiling techniques for targeting commercial advertising. With this, the legislator recognizes, head-on, that practices typical of the economic organization of electronic games may generate specific risks and deserve their own discipline.<1>p. 545</1>

“Art. 20. Loot boxes offered in electronic games directed at children and adolescents are prohibited [...]. Art. 22. [...] the use of profiling techniques for targeting commercial advertising is prohibited [...].” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]c)</2>.<3>p. 545</3>

By prohibiting loot boxes in games directed at children and adolescents, as well as in those likely to be accessed by this audience, the Digital Statute of Children and Adolescents not only abstractly recognized the economic and behavioral sensitivity of this market, but began to interfere in the very form of organization of products previously presented as fully compatible with the presence of minors in the digital ecosystem <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]c)</2>.<3>p. 545</3>

The statute imposes concrete duties to remove content that violates rights and requires a legal representative in the country with powers to receive service of process, while the regulating decree designates an administrative authority, provides for blocking orders and even triggers the technical infrastructural layer of the digital environment through coordination with Anatel and CGI.br. This is important because it dismantles the presentation of the platform as a self-sufficient sovereign space. The digital environment is already an object of public institutionality, with authorities, orders, enforcement mechanisms and mandatory points of contact. Pure self-regulation, in this scenario, poorly describes the state of the law in force.<1>p. 547</1>

“Art. 1 This Decree [...] designates the National Data Protection Agency - ANPD as autonomous administrative authority [...]. Art. 2 The ANPD is designated as the administrative authority [...]. Art. 3 The temporary suspension and the prohibition of the exercise of activities [...] shall be carried out by means of a blocking order.<1>p. 547</1>

BRASIL. Decreto nº 12.622, de 17 de setembro de 2025. Regulamenta a Lei nº 15.211, de 17 de setembro de 2025, para designar a Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados como autoridade administrativa autônoma de proteção de crianças e adolescentes em ambientes digitais, e estabelecer competências para cumprimento de ordens judiciais de bloqueio.<1>p. 806</1>

Bringing its entry into force forward to March 2026 reinforces this point because it shows that the legislator did not treat the matter as a merely symbolic or deferrable agenda, but as a concrete regulatory problem, capable of requiring immediate adaptation by suppliers who structure their activity on microtransaction mechanisms and recurring capture of attention and spending <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2026]b)</2>.<3>p. 545-546</3>
What does Riot's response to the Digital Statute reveal about the object?

Riot Games' reaction to the Digital Statute shows the strength and the limit of sectoral regulation. Instead of immediately reorganizing the economic architecture of League of Legends to keep minors in the game, the company shifted the response to the plane of access. It stated that, in Brazil, minors under 18 cannot access games rated 18+, even with the consent of their guardians, that access reopens upon coming of age or upon reclassification of the game, and that blocked accounts may remain frozen, with items, cosmetics and progress preserved. The response does not delete the account and separates the preservation of records from actual enjoyment.

Riot Games' institutional reaction to the new scenario shows, with special clarity, both the strength and the limit of sectoral regulation. Instead of immediately reorganizing the economic architecture of League of Legends to keep its offer compatible with the continued presence of underage users, the company chose to shift the response to the plane of access, stating that minors could not play titles rated 18+ (for those over eighteen) in Brazil, not even with the consent of their guardians, and linking the eventual restoration of enjoyment to the user's coming of age or to a future reclassification of the game's rating<1>p. 546</1>

In the “Riot Games Parents Portal”, the company clarifies that the guardian may manage account permissions, but not authorize a minor's access to an 18+ title; in addition, it states that accounts barred from accessing such games may remain frozen, with preservation of items, cosmetics, progress and other data linked to the user's history until access is restored <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, [2026]m)</2>. That is, the business response neither deletes the account nor eliminates its digital collection, but separates the preservation of records from actual enjoyment, keeping the patrimonial and historical bond in a state of suspension.<3>p. 546</3>

The episode reads in two directions. On one side, it reveals in an almost confessional way that the value of the relationship is not exhausted in the act of acquisition nor in the abstract ownership of records, because what is in dispute is the continued enjoyment of a position built over time. On the other, it shows that the private response followed the logic of the law of the platform, through the unilateral reengineering of access, preserving the monetization model and transferring to the vulnerable user the practical cost of adaptation. None of this qualifies the response as unlawful, and the sectoral framework is indispensable but not sufficient.

The fact is dogmatically expressive because it reveals, in an almost confessional way, that the value of the consumer relationship is not exhausted in the isolated act of acquisition, nor can it be reduced to the abstract ownership of digital records. What is in dispute is the continued enjoyment of a position built over time, whose utility depends on the user's permanence in the governed environment.<1>p. 546</1>

The episode offers an especially valuable demonstration, since sectoral regulation proves capable of recognizing specific risks and of pressuring the market, but the private response is still organized according to the logic proper to the Lex Plataformae, that is, through the unilateral reengineering of the conditions of access and permanence, and not through spontaneous revision of the economic rationality that produced the problem. The result is revealing. Faced with the application of a public norm aimed at protecting children and adolescents, the platform preserves the monetization model and transfers to the vulnerable user the practical cost of adaptation, turning the former condition of tolerated and economically exploitable participant into a situation of temporary exclusion from the ecosystem.<1>p. 546-547</1>

The methodological importance of this picture lies in showing, with rare clarity, that the sectoral framing of the games market is indispensable, but not sufficient. It sees the risk, names the sector and produces relevant commands; it does not resolve, by itself, the dogmatic problem of continuous enjoyment subjected to opaque, mutable and unilaterally administered private governance.<1>p. 547</1>
How does the sectoral framework relate to the CDC?

In the preliminary reading of the sector, the CDC already appears as a general grammar of protection in mass relationships, and advertising integrated into the game, through storefronts, urgency messages and recommendations, tends to activate the classic instruments of information, transparency and control of abusive practices. The central conflict of the IOC, however, lies in continued provision, architectural opacity, unilateral control of access, the administration of inventories, histories and reputations and evidentiary asymmetry, and none of this disappears because the sector received a name and principles in a statute.
The sectoral framework helps to see the market; it is not enough to control governance.<1>p. 548</1>

The Consumer Protection Code, in this frame, functions as a general grammar of protection in mass relationships marked by informational asymmetry and concentration of the power to organize the offer, without this anticipating, at this point, the specific dogmatic reconstruction of the IOC regime.<1>p. 496</1>

The offer is renewed through events, seasons, promotions, bundles and acquisition incentives built into use, so that advertising also operates as internal communication designed through storefronts, urgency messages, recommendations and highlighting mechanisms. This integration reinforces the continuous and mass character of the supply and tends to activate classic consumer protection instruments aimed at adequate information, transparency and control of abusive practices.<1>p. 495-496</1>

The central conflict remains elsewhere: in continued provision, in architectural opacity, in unilateral control of access, in relevant changes to enjoyment, in the modulation of visibility, in the administration of inventories, histories and reputations, in evidentiary asymmetry and in the private distribution of the conditions of permanence in the ecosystem. None of this disappears because the sector received a name and principles in a statute.<1>p. 548</1>

In IOCs, immaterial product and governed environment are inseparable, and therefore the application of norms must reach administered enjoyment and not be exhausted in the economic-cultural framing of the sector. The insufficiency does not disqualify regulation, which is valuable as a repertoire of recognition, signaling of risks and institutional delimitation, and the missing step is to articulate it with the constitutional economic order, with the CDC and, in tension, with intellectual property, instead of building protection out of a fetish for the games framework. For the lawyer, the sector's statute helps describe the market, but the decisive question remains open before it, namely which limits apply when the platform unilaterally reconfigures access, use, visibility, continuity and functional value equivalence of the immaterial object consumed.

The existence of sectoral regulation does not replace the consumer-law infrastructure, nor does it authorize conflicts of enjoyment to be entirely absorbed by the grammar of the sector or by the language of innovation.<1>p. 548</1>

In IOCs, immaterial product and governed environment are dogmatically inseparable, and therefore the application of norms cannot be exhausted in the economic-cultural framing of the sector. It must reach administered enjoyment and the Lex Plataformae that organizes it. This insufficiency does not disqualify sectoral regulation. It only repositions its reach. The games framework, the protective digital statute and complementary normativity function as an important repertoire of recognition, public signaling of risks and institutional delimitation of the sector.<1>p. 548</1>

The sector may be recognized, promoted and legally named, and still the decisive question may remain open: which limits apply when the platform unilaterally reconfigures access, use, visibility, continuity and functional value equivalence of the immaterial object consumed? It is this question that the sectoral repertoire, alone, does not answer. And it is precisely for this reason that the protection of the IOC must be built not out of a fetish for the “games framework”, but out of the articulation between sectoral regulation, consumer protection, the constitutional economic order and limits on the private exercise of platform powers.<1>p. 548</1>
If the platform is not a State, why does the Constitution apply?

The first objection is that the platform is not a State, and the answer, with Sarlet, is that the reinforced application of fundamental rights does not depend on turning the private party into a quasi-State, it being enough that there is a social and economic power capable of producing relevant subjection. The second is that of acceptance, and Sarmento recalls that the absence of overt coercion does not equal, by itself, real freedom to decide, resist or negotiate. The third is that of free enterprise and innovation, and the answer lies in the constitutional matrix, in which free enterprise is neither a metaphysical right of capital nor a screen for business sovereignty. The fourth is that the reasoning moralizes the market, and the answer, again with Warren and Brandeis, is that reconstructing categories in the face of vulnerability produced at scale is not moralism but a necessary response to keep new forms of power controllable.

Private autonomy, in a constitutional key, is not an abstract safe-conduct for the user's material subjection, especially when inequality of power turns formal freedom into an elegant fiction <1>Sarmento</1><2>(Sarmento, 2010, p. 183; p. 286)</2>. For this reason too, the reinforced application of fundamental rights in the private sphere does not depend on any rite of transforming the private party into a “quasi-State”; it is enough to recognize that the threat to liberty, material equality and dignity may come from holders of social and economic power intense enough to produce relevant subjection <3>Sarlet</3><4>(Sarlet, 2018, p. 527; p. 529; p. 530)</4>.<5>p. 515-516</5>

When the relationship between private parties is organized on non-equal terms, the purely formal invocation of contractual freedom is no longer enough to legitimize the bond, because the absence of overt coercion does not equal, by itself, the existence of real freedom to decide, resist or negotiate under minimally equivalent conditions <1>Sarmento</1><2>(Sarmento, 2010, p. 183)</2>.<3>p. 515</3>

Free enterprise, in this picture, is neither a metaphysical right of capital nor a screen for business sovereignty, but a category functionally conditioned by constitutional purposes and by the protection of the person <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2010, p. 204; p. 208-209)</2>.<3>p. 505-506</3>
Does the platform become a State?

The platform need not be treated as a State for its powers to be legally shapeable, and containment does not require dissolving the private nature of the relationship nor constitutionalizing every private dispute, because it is directed at certain powers exercised through architecture, information and enforcement at scale. Good faith prevents the freedom to shape the bond from becoming private sovereignty, not that freedom from existing. In the Vanguard case, the kernel anti-cheat is not automatically unlawful, the legitimacy of fighting cheating still stands, and what is refused is only the legal immunization of a deep, persistent and opaque technical governance over someone else's machine. The chapter delivers the foundation from which platform governance becomes legally controllable, and the outcome of each case depends on the criteria of the chapters on open auditability, functional value equivalence and the unlawful act of architecture.
The platform need not be treated as a State for its powers to be legally shapeable.<1>p. 513</1>
At the same time, this containment does not require dissolving the private nature of the relationship nor transplanting the legal regime of the State in full to the private party.<1>p. 513</1>

Technical change structurally alters the conditions of exposure, harm and vulnerability, and requires adjustment of categories so that protection remains adherent to the real way in which the conflict is produced. This does not imply equating platform with State nor constitutionalizing every private dispute, but recognizing that certain private powers, when exercised through architecture, information and enforcement at scale, generate asymmetries and risks that are not exhausted in contractual literalness.<1>p. 348</1>
In a platform environment, this prevents the freedom to shape the bond from being turned into private sovereignty over the consumer's position.<1>p. 519</1>
The point here is not to automatically assert the total unlawfulness of the kernel anti-cheat, but to refuse its legal immunization.<1>p. 533</1>

It is not a matter of denying the legitimacy of fighting cheating, but of denying that this legitimacy authorizes, by itself, deep, preventive, persistent and opaque technical governance over someone else's machine.<1>p. 534</1>

The constitutionally legitimate market is one crossed by dignity, social function, repression of abuse and consumer protection, and not one that tries to turn private architecture into a jurisdiction without control. It is from this matrix that there follows the dogmatic possibility of reconstructing, further on, platform governance as a legally controllable phenomenon and of reading the IOC not as an awkward exception to the system, but as one of its hardest contemporary tests.<1>p. 512</1>
